# Module `archive`

archive - gzip / DEFLATE decompression and POSIX tar extraction, in pure Vyb.

Provides `inflate_gzip` (full .gz decode: header, DEFLATE, CRC32 + ISIZE
verification) and `extract_tar` (ustar walk returning member files), so a Vyb
program can turn a fetched `.tar.gz` source into a list of (name, data)
entries byte-identical to the originals.

Byte/bit work uses the String primitives the language ships plus the
single-byte emitter `String::from_byte` (added for #180):
  - read a byte:   `s.char_at(i) & 0xFF`
  - write a byte:  `String::from_byte(b)`  (fresh, owned 1-byte String)
  - accumulate:    `out.concat(chunk)`
This module lives entirely in `stdlib/` as new files and never touches the
runtime/ `src/` (the implementation agent's territory).

Design note: the DEFLATE bit cursor is threaded *functionally* — each decode
step returns a value plus the advanced bit position, and never mutates a
caller-owned cursor. (This shape was first forced by a now-fixed Vyb bug
where re-borrowing a `their` receiver into further `their` calls did not
propagate mutation — see #178; a mutable `their` cursor is now viable, but
threading the position through return values stays simpler and provably
correct, so it is kept.)

Usage:
  import archive::{inflate_gzip, extract_tar}
  match (inflate_gzip(gz_bytes)) {
      plain -> { entries = extract_tar(plain) }
      ?     -> { println("bad gzip") }
  }

<a id="sym-decode_run"></a>
### `decode_run` · fn

```
decode_run(lh<Huff>, dh<Huff>, data<String>, pos<Int>, out<their<Vec<Int>>>)<Int> ->
```

Decode literal/length codes (lh) and distance codes (dh), appending output
into the caller-owned growable byte buffer `out` (a mutable borrow, mutated in
place), until end-of-block (symbol 256). Returns the advanced bit position.
Appends are O(1) amortized on a Vec<Int>: a literal pushes one byte, a
length/distance back-ref pushes `len` bytes read (via get) from the already-
built buffer -- self-referencing overlaps (dist < len) read the just-pushed
bytes, which is correct LZ. This is linear in the inflated byte count, not the
old O(N^2) one-byte String.concat accumulation (#191).
